progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From bio-m7-b01: pathogen, host, bacterium, virus as non-cellular and needing a host cell, tuberculosis caused by a rod-shaped bacterium. From Year 11 (Working Scientifically): independent, dependent and controlled variables, and the purpose of a control. From Module 5 B2c: bacteria multiply by splitting, so a few become a visible crowd. Not assumed: spontaneous generation, miasma, germ theory, the swan-neck design, pure culture, the postulates, correlation against causation, the postulates' limits.
progression.startsWith: Compare Pasteur's and Koch's investigations. The video opens: Leave some broth out for a few days, and it turns cloudy with microbes.
progression.stopsAfter: naming spontaneous generation and miasma as the ideas germ theory replaced, and stating the two things germ theory needed; describing Pasteur's swan-neck experiment (boiled broth, open S-shaped neck, dust settling in the bend, clear broth for months while open straight-necked flasks clouded, cloudy within days after the neck was broken) and explaining why it disproved spontaneous generation (air reached the broth throughout; only particle access changed; the same broth could support growth), with the independent, dependent and controlled variables; stating that Pasteur did not link a microbe to a disease; describing Koch's four steps through his 1882 tuberculosis work (found in every case and not in healthy tissue; grown in pure culture; caused the disease in healthy guinea pigs; recovered again) and explaining why all four are needed (presence only shows association; giving the pure microbe shows cause; recovery rules out another microbe); outlining the limits (viruses need living cells; some bacteria cannot be cultured; healthy carriers; ethics) and the DNA-based alternative; assessing unseen data against the postulates and explaining why they are hard to apply to koala chlamydia.
progression.nextLesson: how a pathogen moves between hosts: direct contact, indirect contact and vectors (route entry bio-m7-b03).

teaching.task: For centuries many people believed microbes sprang from broth and disease came from bad air. How did Pasteur's flasks and Koch's four steps show, instead, that microbes come from other microbes and that a specific microbe causes a specific disease?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why the swan-neck broth stays clear while air reaches it (particles settle in the bend, 3, 4); why the design defeats the "something in the air" objection (air still reaches the broth, 4); why breaking the neck is the critical control (same broth supports growth once particles reach it, 5); why Pasteur did not prove disease causation (no microbe linked to a disease, 6); why presence alone is not proof (the microbe might move in after, 8); why giving the pure microbe shows cause and recovery confirms it (8); why each limit breaks a named step (9). Visible case: three flask states changing by aligned crossfades; dust settling in the bend, then falling into a broken neck; the four step bays filling with real evidence; ticks and gaps on the steps. Thinking opportunities: two unseen items. Reading load: at most about three bright text items; the attempt 1 card with its table is the densest frame and is the task.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Broth left out turns cloudy with microbes, and for centuries many people believed the microbes sprang from the broth and that disease came from bad air, so the question is how Pasteur's flasks and Koch's four steps showed that microbes come from other microbes and that a specific microbe causes a specific disease. Pasteur's swan-neck flasks are traced step by step: boiled broth stays clear for months although air reaches it, answering the claim that boiling or sealing destroyed something in the air, and breaking the neck lets dust fall in so the same broth turns cloudy within days; the variables show what he did and did not show. Koch's tuberculosis work then follows four steps (find it, grow it, give it, find it again) with the reason each is needed, and the postulates' limits are named for viruses, carriers and pathogens that cannot ethically be given to a host. The memory aid matches each scientist to the question he answered. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Leave some broth out for a few days, and it turns cloudy with microbes. For a long time, many people thought those microbes simply sprang from the broth itself, and that disease came from bad air. Around 1860, Louis Pasteur tested the first idea with a flask that let air in but kept microbes out. Then Robert Koch worked out how to prove that one particular microbe causes one particular disease. So how did their experiments establish germ theory?
teaching.understandingCheck: 11a is an assess item: hypothetical data on a lung disease in sheep, where postulates 1 to 3 are met and postulate 4 is missing; assess whether the evidence shows that bacterium X causes the disease. It tests the four steps applied to new data and the correlation trap. 11c is an explain item: Chlamydia pecorum in koalas grows only inside living cells and koalas in New South Wales are listed as endangered; explain two reasons why the postulates are hard to apply. It tests the limits on a new case. Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; the whole card stays on screen during the countdown and after it. Each feedback is brief (about 25 to 30 s): the answer, the key reason, givens underlined in the question strip as they are used, one crossed-out classic mistake. No givens card.
teaching.curriculumScope: B7-IQ1-02: "investigate the work of Robert Koch and Louis Pasteur, to explain the causes and transmission of infectious diseases, including:" with its listed examples "Koch's postulates" and "Pasteur's experiments on microbial contamination". This video covers both listed examples. The ledger flags the dotpoint `depthStudyOrPractical: true`; the video is the secondary-sourced investigation of the two scientists' work (experimental design, controls, results and conclusions). A hands-on contamination experiment is not part of this entry; p02 provides the microbial testing practical. The ledger's investigation component stays open for p02 (microbial contamination practical) and any depth-study entry. Verb demands: "investigate" (scenes 3 to 9 trace each design and its evidence) and "explain" (scenes 6 and 8, and both attempts: why each design licenses its conclusion).

design.visualSystem: One evidence bench: a two-bay board under a banner of two questions. Left bay, "Where do microbes come from?" (Pasteur): a row of painted flasks that changes state by aligned crossfades. Right bay, "Which microbe causes which disease?" (Koch): a strip of four step bays, "find it", "grow it", "give it", "find it again", each filled with painted plates. The left bay builds in scenes 3 to 6 and the right in scenes 7 and 8; scene 9 marks limits on the right bay; scene 10 shows both. Broth changes (clear to cloudy) are aligned plate pairs, never coded tints over a plate; airborne dust and microbes are coded specks drifting along the neck (abstract particles, not organisms). No people, hands, faces, patients or doctors. Sick and healthy hosts that would be people appear only as coded host circles or as tissue on a microscope field. Plates are scaled proportionally, never stretched. Clutter rule (owner, 19 Oct): at most about three bright text items at once besides the small grey bay labels; tags fade when the next cue lands; the bay not being spoken about dims to grey.
